name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,849

clue.text: Fighter provided hints from behind rope on each side

indicators.note: Coming at words 'from behind' means starting at their far end and reading back to their start.
It points at the two flanks of a word, the letter standing at each end with the middle left out.

blocks.note: Hints are TIPS, and the turn writes them back to front.
'Provided' is IF, caught by the same turn and so written backwards.
The two letters standing at the sides of ROPE, its first and its last.

explanation.surface: A boxer calling advice from behind the ropes strung along each side of the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ropes plant a boxing ring in your head, so 'Fighter' reads as a man; it is the wartime aircraft, whose name also belongs to a person of fierce temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spitfire is the Second World War fighter plane, so 'Fighter' names it by exactly what the aircraft was built to be.

clue.text: Shut up and learn, Parisian thought

blocks.note: To pen an animal is to shut it up in an enclosure.
To see that something is so is to learn it — 'I see' when the penny drops.

explanation.surface: Someone told curtly to be quiet and pay attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parisian' is the standard signal that the answer is the French word rather than the English one, and the grid quietly drops the accent from pensée.
explanation.definitionFit: Pensée is French for a thought, which is what 'Parisian' asks for — the same idea in the other language.

clue.text: Sandwich sample filled with bits separately

indicators.note: A filling goes inside its case, so what follows is pushed into the middle of the word named before it.
It says the two go in at different points rather than being dropped in together as a pair.

blocks.note: To sample something is to taste it.
Bits here are binary digits, 0 and 1, and O and I are the letters they are written as.

explanation.surface: A tasting sample of a sandwich, stuffed with assorted bits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bits' is computing, not crumbs: a bit is a binary digit, and the setter hands over the two of them as the letters they look like.
explanation.definitionFit: A toastie is a toasted sandwich, so 'Sandwich' defines it by the wider class of food it belongs to.

clue.text: Suggest taking top off only

indicators.note: In a down entry the top is the opening letter, and taking it off strips it from the front.

blocks.note: 'Only' in the sense of merely is SIMPLY, and the letter at its top comes away.

explanation.surface: Advice to take the top off and nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' is not a lid here but the first letter of a word written down the grid, and 'Suggest' stands apart as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply something is to suggest it without stating it — the same verb, stopping one step short of saying it.

clue.text: Dogs seen swimming across river caught up

indicators.note: Something swimming is drifting loose in the water, so its letters will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight of the nine letters
r = river, the abbreviation printed on maps

explanation.surface: Dogs paddling across a river while somebody watches from the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last two words, and 'caught up' means absorbed in something, not snagged on it — which is where the swimming pushes you.
explanation.definitionFit: To be caught up in a book is to be absorbed in it, which is this word's sense — not caught up as in overtaken.

clue.text: Increase already high level of canine dedication?

blocks.note: A dedication at the front of a book opens with the word 'To'.
A pup is a young canine.

explanation.surface: A question about whether a dog's already boundless devotion could be raised any higher.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the five letters after the second one and the answer reads as the opening of a dedication addressed to a dog, which is what the question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: To top up is to add more to a level that is already part-way there — a refill rather than a first filling.

clue.text: Catch close to fence after American's easy swing

indicators.note: It sets the letter it introduces behind the piece just named.

blocks.note: A trap catches an animal, and to catch is to trap.
Americans write easy as E-Z, as on the E-Z Pass toll lanes.
The close of 'fence' is the letter it ends on.

explanation.surface: A baseball catch taken near the fence off an American's lazy swing of the bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swing' is the batter's swing in the surface and a piece of circus apparatus in the answer — a bar hung on two ropes.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapeze is literally a swing: the bar an acrobat hangs from and swings on, high above the ring.

clue.text: Deep hole revolutionary digs for attacks

blocks.note: A pit is a deep hole.
Che Guevara is the crossword's standard revolutionary.
In the slang sense, someone who digs a thing is into it — so 'revolutionary digs' becomes 'Che's into'.

explanation.surface: A revolutionary digging himself a deep trench to attack from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like the spadework in the surface and is really the sixties slang for being keen on something, which is how three words hand over four pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch into someone is to set about them, with fists or with words — an attack rather than a mere complaint.

clue.text: Cactus is sort of ecotype that avoids cold

indicators.note: Read as an instruction to sort, it asks for the letters put into a different order.
It keeps one letter out of the mix altogether rather than shuffling it in with the others.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, once the cold letter has been kept out
c = cold, the letter on the tap, and it is the one dropped

explanation.surface: A plant described as a variety that cannot stand the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Botanical vocabulary is the disguise: an ecotype is a genuine term for a locally adapted population, sitting there in plain sight to be taken apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Peyote is a small spineless cactus of Mexico and the Texas borderlands, best known for the mescaline in it.

clue.text: God's gift, guy already taken?

blocks.note: A guy is a man.
Something already taken is not available — N/A on any form.

explanation.surface: A dating lament: the perfect fellow turns out to be spoken for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God's gift' is the man who thinks himself irresistible in the surface, and in the answer it is the food that fell from heaven for the Israelites.
explanation.definitionFit: Manna is the food God sent the Israelites in the wilderness, so 'God's gift' names it by where it came from.

clue.text: US entreés including tip for table service

indicators.note: What is included is taken inside, so the single letter goes into the middle of the word before it.
A tip is the point a thing starts at, and here that is the letter the following word begins with.

blocks.note: In America the entrée is the main course, so American entrées are mains.
Nothing looked up here: it is the first letter of the word, taken as its tip.

explanation.surface: A restaurant bill for American main courses with a tip added for the table service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' is a church service and not a waiter's: matins is morning prayer, which the restaurant surface is built to keep out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Matins is the morning service of the Anglican church, so 'service' names it by the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Display article and essay on piece of paper

indicators.note: In an across clue it names what the earlier pieces rest on, so the sheet comes first and they follow it.

blocks.note: A page is a piece of paper.
AN is the indefinite article.
To essay something is to try it — the verb, not the schoolwork.

explanation.surface: A writer fitting an article and an essay onto a single sheet of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' hides best of the three: read as a noun it belongs with 'article' in the surface, and as a verb it means to attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Pageantry is showy display — processions, costume and ceremony staged to be looked at.

clue.text: You shouldn't have left going into town without saying anything

indicators.note: It sends the letter before it inside the word named next, rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: 'Ta' is British informal for thanks, what you say on being handed a present.
A city is a town.
l = left, the standard abbreviation.

explanation.surface: A reproach to somebody who set off for town without a word to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is the polite noise made over a gift, not a telling-off, and the surface exists to make you read it as the telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something tacitly is to do it unspoken — agreement understood rather than said aloud.

clue.text: Pets Charles keeps at home have a relaxed time

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, so the name closes around the pieces that follow.

blocks.note: Chas is the familiar short form of Charles.
Somebody at home is in.
To chill is to have a relaxed time.

explanation.surface: Charles taking it easy indoors with the animals he looks after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' does both jobs at once: Charles looking after animals in the surface, and one word holding others inside it in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinchillas are South American rodents with famously soft fur, kept in this country as household pets.

clue.text: Send the ball long on smash

blocks.note: A row on money is a row over money — the two prepositions do the same job.
A smash is a hit, on the tennis court and in the charts.

explanation.surface: A cricket ball smashed away towards long on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long on' is a real fielding position and the surface leans hard on it; the definition stops at 'long', and the two words after it are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To overhit is to strike the ball harder than intended so it travels too far — sending it long.

clue.text: Silence grunting player getting in top seed's head

blocks.note: The top seed is the No. 1, and 'No. 1's' spells out as NO, the Roman numeral for one, and S.
Monica Seles, the tennis champion whose loud grunting on court was famous enough to be a story in itself.
A ness is a headland, which makes 'head' the usual way of asking for it.

explanation.surface: A grunting opponent getting under the top seed's skin, and a call for her to be quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting in someone's head is the sports-psychology cliché the surface runs on, and it doubles as the literal instruction to go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Noiselessness is the state of making no noise at all, which is what 'Silence' names as a noun.

clue.text: Old judge under cover with flags raised is dry

indicators.note: In a down entry, raised letters are read bottom to top, so the word arrives the wrong way round.

blocks.note: To cover ground with flags is to PAVE it — flags are flagstones — and the word is then read upwards.
o = old, the standard abbreviation.
To rate something is to judge it.

explanation.surface: An elderly judge under a canopy with the flags run up above him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flags' are paving stones, not bunting, and the clue spends its whole surface pointing at the flagpole instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To dry is what a puddle does when it evaporates — the water leaves as vapour, so the definition names the process by its result.

clue.text: Fellow behind vehicle causing tailback, perhaps

blocks.note: A fellow is a he.
Somebody's behind is their backside, and this is the blunt British word for it.

explanation.surface: A man walking behind a slow vehicle while the traffic piles up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' is the noun and not the preposition, which is why the clue reads so smoothly as a fellow standing at the back of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearse leads a funeral procession at walking pace, so it is one vehicle apt to cause a tailback — the British word for a long traffic queue.

clue.text: Two things you get from overpaid butcher show inconsistency

blocks.note: A chop is the cut of meat you go to a butcher for.
Two things named together are joined by 'and', which is the middle word here.
Hand over too much money and you get change back.

explanation.surface: A shopper handing the butcher rather more money than the meat costs.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a shopping list rather than a set of instructions — the pieces are simply what the counter hands back, with the joining word supplied by 'two'.
explanation.definitionFit: To chop and change is to keep altering your plans, so the phrase means inconsistency in behaviour and cuts nothing at all.

clue.text: Part-time queen not as expensive

blocks.note: Part-time work goes on and off rather than running continuously.
ER = Elizabeth Regina, the crossword's standard queen.

explanation.surface: A monarch who works only part of the week, and costs the country less for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a price and not a person: goods on offer are the ones with money knocked off, which the cut-price royal keeps you from seeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods on offer are being sold at a reduced price, which is the shop-window sense of 'not as expensive'.

clue.text: Upset since doctor I see is difficult to get hold of

indicators.note: Upset means tipped over, and in a down entry that writes the pieces from the bottom of the column up.

blocks.note: 'Now you mention it' and 'since you mention it' do the same job — now can stand for since.
dr = doctor, the standard title.
'Ah' is the noise you make when you see the point.

explanation.surface: A patient complaining that their own doctor is never available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as the patient's mood and works as the instruction to turn three small pieces over.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hard-won took real effort to obtain, so it is difficult to get hold of in the sense of difficult to come by.

clue.text: Internet-based catastrophe stopped by odd bits of tech

indicators.note: Being stopped by something is being blocked in mid-flow, so those letters sit inside the word.
'Odd' counts positions rather than describing oddity: the first and third letters, taken as they come.

blocks.note: Doom is catastrophe — the fate rather than the event.
The letters in the odd positions of the word, its first and third.

explanation.surface: An online catastrophe halted by a few stray bits of technology.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the first word and reads as part of the disaster story; the label attaches to any firm whose business address ends in .com.
explanation.definitionFit: A dotcom is a company that trades on the internet, named after the .com at the end of its web address.

clue.text: Venezuelan water company started by several stars switching on

indicators.note: 'Switching' asks two letters to trade places and 'on' names exactly which two are to swap.
It says the firm has the other piece in front of it, standing at the start.

blocks.note: Orion is the constellation, several stars taken together, with the ON at its end swapped round.
co = company, as at the end of a firm's name.

explanation.surface: A Venezuelan water company set up by a group of celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' are the celebrity kind in the surface and the astronomical kind in the wordplay — the hunter, the best-known constellation of them all.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orinoco is one of South America's great rivers, running through Venezuela, so 'Venezuelan water' names it by country and kind.

clue.text: Free running stream swamps shelter during flood

indicators.note: To swamp a thing is to close over it entirely.

blocks.note: A pour is a stream of liquid.
Noah's ark is the shelter built to ride out the Flood.

explanation.surface: A river in spate overwhelming the last shelter left standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free running' opens the clue looking like water running freely and names the urban sport of vaulting walls and railings at speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkour is the discipline of crossing city obstacles at a run, and free running is the English name for the same thing.

clue.text: Playing padel, say in court?

indicators.note: Playing at a thing is not doing it straight, so the letters come out in some other order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder — padel is the racquet sport played on a small glass-walled court

explanation.surface: A game of padel under way on court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks as though it is flagging an example or a sound-alike, and it belongs to the definition: by the last word the court is a court of law.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to state your case in court — guilty or not guilty is the first thing a defendant says there.

clue.text: Garden shelter made for Carol's outside being reassembled

indicators.note: It takes the letters standing at the two ends of the name and leaves the middle where it is.
Something reassembled is put back together in a fresh arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
The letters at the outside of CAROL, its first and its last.

explanation.surface: A shelter built for Carol in the garden, taken to pieces and put back together.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is hiding as joinery: 'made for' looks like the words holding the sentence up, and it supplies seven of the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold frame is the low glass-topped box a gardener raises seedlings in — a shelter for plants rather than people.

clue.text: Hearing trouser measurement, lose a lot of weight

indicators.note: It asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, so you write down what reaches the ear.

blocks.note: The measurement round a pair of trousers is the WAIST, and that sound has a second spelling.

explanation.surface: Somebody hearing their trouser size read out and resolving to slim.
explanation.walkthrough: One sound, two spellings: the tailor's measurement is the WAIST, and the definition wants the other one — to waste is to grow thin, as in wasting away.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste is to lose flesh and weight through illness or hunger — the sense in 'waste away', not the squandering one.

clue.text: See 2
Mize reportedly back on Tour? He's unlikely to chip in

indicators.note: A name reported is passed on as a sound, so you write down what you hear rather than how it is spelt.
It asks for the letter at the rear of the word, the one it finishes on.

blocks.note: Larry Mize is the American golfer who won the 1987 Masters, and his name said aloud can be written with an S.
The letter at the back of 'Tour'.

explanation.surface: A golfer said to be back on tour, and no use at all in a whip-round.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf runs through the whole clue: a chip is the short lofted shot played near the green, while chipping in also means paying your share.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser hoards his money and will not contribute, so the definition describes him by the thing he refuses to do.

clue.text: Risk outrage putting finale first

indicators.note: It sends the ending round to the front, ahead of the word it would otherwise follow.

blocks.note: A finale is the end of a performance.
Outrage is anger — the feeling rather than the act that provokes it.

explanation.surface: A promoter chancing an uproar by moving the finale to the top of the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Risk' and 'outrage' sit together as though the clue were about a decision certain to annoy people, and only the first of them is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger something is to put it at risk — the two verbs take the same object: you endanger, or risk, your health.
